en: The Diamond Cutter Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
translated during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Guptadharma.
Homage to all Buddhas and the ocean-like assembly of Bodhisattvas!
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Blessed One was wandering among the Śroṇāparāntakas in the Jeta Grove, the park of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering five hundred.
At that time, during the forenoon, the Blessed One put on his lower robe, took up his bowl and outer robe, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī for alms.

Having walked through the great city of Śrāvastī for alms, finished his meal, and concluded his post-meal duties, he set aside his bowl and outer robe, washed both feet, and prepared his sitting mat. Thus seated upon it, he sat cross-legged, straightened his body, and established mindfulness before him.
At that time, many bhikṣus, having approached the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and sat down to one side.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti was seated among that great assembly.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder,
knelt with his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One in this way:
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
All that there is of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas being favorably received by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the most excellent favorable reception;
all that there is of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas entrusting [the Dharma] to Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is the most excellent entrustment.”
"World-Honored One, how should one who has set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle abide?
How should they practice?"
"What is the method for subduing the mind?
When he had spoken thus,
the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:
“Excellent, excellent,
Subhūti! It is so, it is so!”
“Subhūti! It is so, it is so!
This is the most excellent way of attracting and gathering followers among all those practiced by Tathāgatas and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
The entrustment: This is the most supreme entrustment of the Tathāgata to the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Listen well, Subhūti!
Pay close attention and bear it in mind; I shall speak of how a bodhisattva who has set out in the vehicle should abide, how they should practice, and how they should subdue their minds.
"So be it, World-Honored One! the Venerable Subhūti replied,
"I wish to hear it from the World-Honored One."
The Blessed One said this: "In this regard,
Subhūti, one who has set out on the bodhisattva vehicle should generate the mind in this way:"

"Subhūti, whatever sentient beings there are—comprehensively included within the category of 'sentient beings,' whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or formless; whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither percipient nor non-percipient—all those who are designated as belonging to the realm of sentient beings, I shall all lead to parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder."
"In this way, although immeasurable sentient beings have been brought to parinirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has been brought to parinirvāṇa.
For what reason? If, Subhūti!"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva has turned away from the notion of a "sentient being," it is not appropriate to call him a "bodhisattva mahāsattva.
For what reason? It is because, Subhūti, he is not [a bodhisattva].
A Bodhisattva is called "one who speaks appropriately" if they transform the perception of a sentient being, or transform the perception of a life-span, or transform the perception of a person.
Nevertheless, furthermore, Subhūti!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice giving while not abiding in things; they should practice giving while abiding in nothing; they should practice giving while not abiding in form; and they should practice giving while not abiding in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
In this way, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice giving while abiding in the non-perception of signs.
For what reason?
If, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell upon giving, then, Subhūti,
the mass of merit he thereby acquires is immeasurable.
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Can the extent of space in front of one be grasped?"
Subhūti said: “It is not so, World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"In this way, [taking] from the right, south, behind, west, high, north, below, above, and in the intermediate directions—could one grasp the measure of space throughout the ten directions?
Subhūti said: "Not so, World-Honored One!"
The Blessed One said:
“So it is, so it is, Subhūti!”
"So it is, so it is! Subhūti,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not dwell upon the act of giving,
the mass of merit that he thereby receives is immeasurable."
Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva who has set out in the vehicle practices giving, he should abide even in the notion of non-apprehension.
What do you think?
“Subhūti,
can a Tathāgata be seen by means of the possession of marks?
Subhūti replied:
"No, Blessed One! One should not perceive a Tathāgata by means of the possession of marks.
For what reason?
"If that were so, the Tathāgata would be one who possesses the marks of physical perfection;
yet he is not one who possesses such marks.
When this had been said, [the Buddha replied: "So it is."
World-Honored One, the Venerable Subhūti spoke thus:
"Whatever, Subhūti, is the possession of marks, that is false;
whatever is the non-possession of marks, that is not false. This mark and non-mark should be seen by the Tathāgata."
When this had been said,
the venerable Subhūti spoke thus to the Blessed One:
“Nevertheless, Blessed One!”

Will there be any sentient beings who, in a future time, at a later period, during the final five-hundred-year phase when the True Dharma is being destroyed and the era has shifted—within this very context, regarding the teachings spoken in such sūtras as these—will give rise to the perception that they are real?
The Blessed One said:
"Do not, Subhūti, speak in such a manner."
"Nevertheless, World-Honored One, will there be sentient beings in the future,

at a later time, a later long period, during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is being destroyed and its era has turned, who— within such sūtras as these that have been spoken— will give rise to the perception of reality?"
"Nevertheless, furthermore, Subhūti, in the future there will be a time,

during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is being destroyed and the era is turning, in which there will be bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have reached the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of merit, and the perfection of wisdom."
"No, furthermore, Subhūti, at that time,
those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will have attended upon and made offerings to only a single Buddha, and they will not have planted roots of merit under many Buddhas."
Furthermore, Subhūti,

although those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas may not have attended upon and made offerings to hundreds of thousands of buddhas, nor planted roots of goodness under hundreds of thousands of buddhas, they shall nevertheless come to possess single-minded pure faith when this discourse on the Dharma— spoken within such categories of sūtras— is being taught.
Subhūti, it is through the Tathāgata’s buddha-wisdom that he knows them;
Subhūti, it is through [that wisdom] that he sees them.
Subhūti, all those immeasurable masses of merit will be produced and should be grasped by the Tathāgata’s Buddha-eye.
For what reason? It is because, Subhūti,
those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not give rise to the notion of a self, nor do they give rise to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, or the notion of a person.
Furthermore, Subhūti, do those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas not give rise to the notion of phenomena, nor do they give rise to the notion of non-phenomena; furthermore,
do they not give rise to the notion of perception, nor the notion of non-perception?
For what reason? If, Subhūti,

those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were to give rise to the notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*), they would likewise have the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), the grasping at a sentient being (*sattva-grāha*), the grasping at a life-force (*jīva-grāha*), and the grasping at a person (*pudgala-grāha*).
If the perception of a phenomenon does not arise, for such a person there would be the grasping of a self, the grasping of a sentient being, the grasping of a life-span, and the grasping of a person.
What is the reason for this?
"No, moreover, Subhūti!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should grasp the Dharma, not grasp what is non-Dharma.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has taught the parable of the raft as a means of understanding the Dharma; even the Dharma should be relinquished, how much more so what is non-Dharma."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One, the Venerable Subhūti spoke thus:
'What do you think, Subhūti?'"
"Is there a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha who has realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment?
Or is there any dharma that the Tathāgata has taught? Subhūti replied:
“As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, O Blessed One, there is not a single dharma that the Tathāgata has realized through his unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening;
nor is there a single dharma that the Tathāgata has taught.”
What is the reason for this?
If that which the Tathāgata has taught as the Dharma is ungraspable, it is ineffable; it is not that Dharma, nor is it non-Dharma.
"For what reason?
Because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) manifest the noble ones (*ārya*).
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?

If some son of good family or daughter of good family were to fill this trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and offer it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas; [would that person on that basis generate much merit?]"
What do you think, Subhūti?
Would a great mass of merit arise for that son of good family or daughter of good family on account of that?
Subhūti said:
“Much, World-Honored One! Much, Sugata!”
That son of good family, or daughter of good family, will generate a great mass of merit on that account!
For what reason?
Because of that, Blessed One!
"A mass of merit;
yet the Tathāgata has said it is not a mass.
Why is that, Blessed One?"
"The Tathāgata has spoken of 'a mass of merit, a mass of merit,' Subhūti.
The Blessed One said:
"Furthermore, Subhūti!"
Noble son, or noble daughter, if one were to fill this trichiliocosm with the seven precious treasures and offer it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas;

If one receives even as little as a four-line verse from this Dharma-fundamental and, for the sake of others, explains it in detail and analyzes it, from that cause and condition, a vast mass of merit will arise—immeasurable and incalculable.
For what reason is that? It is because, Subhūti,
from this [perfection] has come forth the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and the unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment.
In this world, there have been Buddhas, World-Honored Ones.
What is the reason for that?
Subhūti, as for "Buddha-dharma, Buddha-dharma," [it is thus].
"That which is not the Buddha-dharma is thus;
because of that, it is called 'Buddha-dharma,'" the World-Honored One said.
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Nevertheless, one should form such a thought regarding the influxes: "
"‘I have attained the fruit of stream-entry’?
Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
For what reason?
It is not so, World-Honored One!"
Because he does not enter the sphere of form,
nor the spheres of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena, for that reason he is called one who has entered the stream.
If, World-Honored One,
that person should give rise to such a thought:
"I have attained the fruit of stream-entry."
"In that way, for him, there exists the grasping at a self, the grasping at a sentient being, the grasping at a life-force, and the grasping at a person.
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think?"
"Subhūti!
Nevertheless, a once-returner should think thus:
'I have attained the fruit of once-returning.'"
Subhūti said: "It is not so, World-Honored One!"
What is the reason for this?
It is not that he thinks:
"I have attained the fruit of once-returning."
“What is the reason for this?
It is because there is no dharma [in him] that constitutes a once-returner; therefore, he is called a ‘once-returner.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Nevertheless, he does not form such a thought: [that he has come]."
"Have I attained the fruit of non-returning?
Subhūti replied:
"Not so, Blessed One! For what reason?
Because there is no dharma therein that has not come and entered; for that reason, he is called 'one who does not come'."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
Nevertheless, one should think thus: "I shall attain it."
Subhūti said: "It is not so, World-Honored One!
For what reason?"
"No, World-Honored One!
If there were a dharma that should be called 'corresponding,' for that reason one would say it is 'corresponding.
But if, World-Honored One,"
One should reflect thus:
"I shall attain it.
In this way, there exists for him the grasping at a self, the grasping at a sentient being, the grasping at a life-span, and the grasping at a person.
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, this Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the supreme practice of non-contention; for this reason, Blessed One, I—this [person]—[am so].
"One should be free from desire. It is not 'I,' O Bhagavān!
Thus one should reflect.
"Regarding this 'I am worthy': World-Honored One,
if I were to think thus:"
"I should attain it.
To me, the Tathāgata has declared:
"The practice of non-contention is supreme."
"Subhūti! Because a son of good family has no sphere of activity, he is therefore called 'one who practices without conflict' (araṇā-vihārin), a practitioner of non-conflict.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Is there even a single dharma that the Tathāgata, having become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has taken up?"
Subhūti said: “It is not so, World-Honored One!
There is not a single dharma that the Tathāgata, having become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, has taken up.”
The Blessed One said: “If,
Subhūti, there should be a bodhisattva mahāsattva who speaks thus:”
"My buddha-field is accomplished with such adornments.
This statement of his is not as it says.
For what reason?
"Subhūti, as for the adornment of the buddha-field,
the Tathāgata has said it is non-adornment; therefore,
it is called the 'adornment of the buddha-field'."
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thus give rise to a mind that does not dwell;
he should give rise to a mind that does not dwell on form, nor on sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, or mental phenomena; he should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere!
“Suppose, Subhūti, a man were to have a physical form such as this, like that of Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think?
[Would he have a large body?]”
“Subhūti, nevertheless, does that great self-body exist?
Subhūti replied:
“Great, World-Honored One! Great, Sugata!
That self-body exists.”
For what reason?
"Self" or "one who has a self," World-Honored One—that does not exist;
it was spoken of by the Tathāgata as such.
For that reason, it is called "my body.
It does not exist, Blessed One! It is not that.
"For that reason, it is called 'my body.
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think?"
"Subhūti! As many grains of sand as there are in all those great rivers, the Ganges—would those grains of sand be numerous?"
Subhūti said: "So many as those, World-Honored One, are the great Ganges Rivers that exist; how much more so the sands within them?"
The Blessed One said:
"I desire you, Subhūti;
I know you, Subhūti."

Suppose there were as many worlds as there are grains of sand in all those great rivers of the Ganges; and suppose a woman or a man were to fill them with the seven precious treasures and offer them to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Would a great mass of merit arise from that woman, or from that man, or from those conditions?"
Subhūti said:
“Much, World-Honored One! Much, Sugata!”
“Whether it be that woman, or that man, or the conditions thereof, a great mass of merit is produced—immeasurable and incalculable.
The Blessed One said:
“Furthermore, at that time, Subhūti!”
Noble son, or noble daughter, if one were to fill those worlds with the seven precious jewels and offer them as gifts to the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and so forth.

If one receives even as much as a single four-line verse from this Dharma-fundamental and, having received it, explains it in detail and analyzes it for others, by such causes and conditions, a vast mass of merit will arise—immeasurable and incalculable!
Furthermore, Subhūti, at that time, in this region,
if this discourse on the Dharma— even as much as a single four-line verse— is explained to others, analyzed, or expounded in detail, then that region will be honored by gods, humans, and asuras.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
if this discourse on the Dharma is upheld, read, recited, and explained in detail for others, it will possess the most supreme and rare excellence.
"In this regard, Subhūti,
the Teacher’s wandering through various regions, his honoring of those worthy of respect, and his shared practice of the holy life (brahmacarya) are similar. Thus he spoke.
Then the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One in this way:
"What, Blessed One, is the name of this 'Dharma-fundamental'?"
"How, and in what manner, do you uphold me?
When he had spoken thus,
the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti:
“‘The Perfection of Wisdom’—this, Subhūti, is the name of this very dharma-gate;
thus it should be upheld.
For what reason? Because...”
If it is so, Subhūti, that one has reached the perfection of wisdom,
the Tathāgata says that such a person has not, in reality, reached the perfection of wisdom.
For that reason, he is called one who has reached the other shore of wisdom.
What do you think, Subhūti?
"Nevertheless, is there any dharma such as that which the Tathāgata has taught?
Subhūti replied, "Not so, World-Honored One!"
"No, World-Honored One!
There is no such dharma as that which the Tathāgata speaks of.
The World-Honored One said:
“Subhūti, how much dust of the earth is there in all the three-thousandfold world-system?
Subhūti replied:
“Very many, Blessed One!
Very many, Sugata!
Those particles of earth.”
For what reason?
If, World-Honored One,
that which is called "earth-dust" by the Tathāgata—
That which is not dust, the Tathāgata has called it;
for that reason, it is designated by the name "dust of the earth.
That which is a world, the Tathāgata has called it.
"It is 'not a world' that the Tathāgata has preached;
for that reason, it is called a 'world.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Should the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha be seen by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?"
Subhūti said: “It is not so, World-Honored One!
It is not by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is to be seen.”
For what reason is this?
World-Honored One,
as for those thirty-two marks of a great man that the Tathāgata has spoken of;
"The Tathāgata has said that these marks do not exist as such;
for that reason, they are called the 'thirty-two marks of a great man.
The World-Honored One said:

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if at any time a woman or a man were to give up their own bodies as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River every day, and were to give up their own bodies in this manner for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and if someone else, having received even a single four-line verse from this Dharma-discourse, were to analyze and explain it to others—this latter person would, by that cause and condition, generate a far greater mass of merit, immeasurable and incalculable."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti, his tears falling due to the power of the Dharma being swiftly turned, wiped those tears away and addressed the Blessed One in this way:
“It is marvelous, Blessed One!”
Most excellent and marvelous, O Sugata!
This Dharma-discourse which the Tathāgata has spoken—this, World-Honored One, is born of wisdom;
never before in my life have I heard such a Dharma-discourse as this.
"Most Excellent One! World-Honored One!
It is rare for sentient beings to possess such merit that, when this sutra is preached, a perception of reality arises within them."
For what reason? Because,
World-Honored One, this is indeed a perception of reality.
"It is thus for him that there is no perception;
for that reason, the Tathāgata speaks of 'true perception,' and one who has true perception.
It is not 'self,' Blessed One!"
It is rare! If,
within this discourse on the root of my Dharma, they have faith in me and understand me—
if, O World-Honored One, they do so— then [they shall attain liberation].

There will be sentient beings in future ages who shall receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this fundamental dharma-text in detail to others; they shall be endowed with the most supreme and rare qualities.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
at that time those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas will not give rise to the notion of a self, nor will they give rise to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, or the notion of a person.
What is the reason for this?
If, Blessed One, that which is my notion of self is, in such a way, not a notion;
If one possesses such notions of a sentient being, a life-span, or a person, those are not, in fact, notions.
For what reason?
Because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the complete relinquishing of all notions.
When he had spoken thus,
the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: “So it is, so it is!
"Subhūti! So it is, so it is!
Just as you have said."
Those sentient beings who possess such supreme and rare merit shall, when this discourse is preached within this sutra, not be startled, not be terrified, and not be afraid.
For what reason? Subhūti,
it is because the Tathāgata has spoken of this as "reaching the most excellent further shore."
Furthermore, Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata,
having reached the supreme perfection, has taught— that immeasurable [perfection] has also been taught by the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Ones; for that reason, it is called "the one who has reached the supreme perfection."
"Furthermore, Subhūti, although the Tathāgata has reached the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), he has not, in that sense, reached a 'perfection.
For what reason? "

At that time, Subhūti, when the wicked king cut and divided my flesh, at that moment I did not have the notion of a self, nor the notion of a sentient being, nor the notion of a life-span, nor the notion of a person; I had neither the notion of a non-self nor the notion of no-notion.
For what reason? If, Subhūti,
the notion of a self were present in that state,
the notion of malice would also be present in that state for me.
Subhūti, when the notions of a sentient being, a life-span, or a person existed, and the notion of malice also existed within me at that time, I was mindful and aware:

"In the past, during five hundred births, when I was a rishi who practiced patience, even then I had no notion of a self, no notion of a sentient being, no notion of a life-span, and no notion of a person; nor did I have any notion of existence or non-existence."
Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should give up all conceptualizations;

they should generate a mind directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, yet they should not generate a mind that dwells on form, nor should they generate a mind that dwells on sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles; they should not generate a mind that dwells on phenomena, nor should they generate a mind that dwells on the absence of phenomena; they should generate a mind that is non-abiding.
What is the reason for this?

If there is no dwelling, he dwells in such a way; therefore, the Tathāgata has said that a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice giving without dwelling on form, and should practice giving without dwelling on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice such giving for the sake of all sentient beings.
For what reason? "
If it is so, Subhūti, that which is called the "conception of a sentient being" is, in fact, not a conception. If it is so,
those whom the Tathāgata has described as "all sentient beings" are, in fact, not sentient beings.
For what reason?
Because, Subhūti, the Tathāgata speaks the truth;
the Tathāgata speaks reality; the Tathāgata does not speak otherwise; the Tathāgata speaks according to how things are; the Tathāgata does not speak contrary to how things are.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, whether the Tathāgata has awakened to and taught the Dharma,
or whether one contemplates it, therein there is neither truth nor falsehood."
For example, Subhūti,
it is as if a man enters a dark house and does not see anything at all.
In the same way, a bodhisattva should view things as falling into [the category of] phenomena, if they fall into the practice of giving.
For example, Subhūti,
just as a man with sight sees various forms when the bright moon rises at night,
so too should a bodhisattva mahāsattva see; he does not fall into [the notion of] things as being given.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, if sons of good family or daughters of good family should receive,
uphold, read, recite, and explain this discourse on dharma in detail for others, [they will produce a great deal of merit]."
Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows that through his Buddha-wisdom;
Subhūti, he sees that.
Subhūti, by means of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-eye,
all those sentient beings shall generate and take up an immeasurable mass of merit.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,

if at some time a woman or a man were to sacrifice bodies equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River during the first watch of the day, and likewise during the middle watch, and likewise during the last watch of the day, sacrificing bodies equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River."
For this reason, throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, I have sacrificed my own body.
If, upon hearing this fundamental dharma, one does not slander it, then by such causes and conditions, a mass of merit far exceeding that will arise—immeasurable and incalculable.
Why, moreover, do you say that one who has copied it, and then receives, maintains, recites, and reads it, and for the sake of others and so forth explains it in detail?
"Nevertheless, furthermore, at that time, Subhūti!"
It is inconceivable and incomparable; this is the fundamental nature of dharmas. That is inconceivable, and thus it should be observed as its fruit. This, Subhūti!

This Dharma-fundamental was taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of those beings who have set out upon the supreme vehicle, and for the sake of those beings who have set out upon the most excellent vehicle.
If one should receive, uphold, read, and recite this Dharma-fundamental, and should explain it extensively and analytically for others, [one shall attain great merit].
Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows that through his buddha-wisdom;
Subhūti, he sees that.
Subhūti, all those sentient beings will possess an immeasurable mass of merit; they will possess an inconceivable, incomparable, and unquantifiable mass of merit.
"Subhūti, all those sentient beings shall carry the bodhi of the Tathāgata upon their shoulders! Why is that?"

"No, Subhūti! If beings of inferior faith and understanding were to hear this fundamental Dharma, it is impossible that they could hear, receive, uphold, read, or recite it—unless they are those who do not perceive a self, do not perceive a being, do not perceive a life-span, and do not perceive a person, and who have made the vow of a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, Subhūti, this region where this sutra is extensively taught shall be honored by the worlds of devas, humans, and asuras; they shall pay homage to it, circumambulate it to the right, and treat that region as if it were a caitya."
“Furthermore, Subhūti,
if any son of good family or daughter of good family should receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this kind of sūtra in detail for others, they will be despised and utterly reviled.”
What is the reason for this?
It is because those sentient beings, having committed unwholesome karma in their previous lives, have fallen into the miserable realms;
yet, by undergoing such contempt within these present phenomena, they shall eventually attain the awakening of a Buddha.
"For what reason?

Because, Subhūti, I remember that in the past, incalculable and beyond counting eons ago, there were Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—more than four, eight, ten, twenty, even hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas—who were personally attended and honored by me; having personally attended and honored them, I did not depart from them."

If, Subhūti, I were to personally attend upon and make offerings to those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and never depart from them, yet were to receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain this sūtra for others and analyze it in detail during a later time, a later long period, in the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is being destroyed and the era is changing; [then my merit would be greater].

Furthermore, Subhūti, at that time, compared to this mass of merit, the previous mass of merit does not even approach a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a koṭī-hundred-thousandth part, nor a koṭī-nayuta-hundred-thousandth part; it does not even bear comparison by way of calculation, or a fraction, or a number, or a metaphor, or an upaniṣad, nor even by way of a simile.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, regarding those sons of good family and daughters of good family, I shall speak of their mass of merit: if those sons of good family and daughters of good family were to take up that mass of merit during that time, fierce beings would approach them and their minds would become deranged."
Furthermore, Subhūti, although the Tathāgata has preached the dharmas as inconceivable and incomparable, one should observe that their fruit is likewise inconceivable.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One in this way:
“How, Blessed One, should one who has set out in the vehicle of the bodhisattva dwell?”
"How should one practice the response?
How is the mind to be subdued?
The World-Honored One said:
"In this regard, Subhūti, one who has set out on the bodhisattva vehicle should give rise to such a thought:

'All sentient beings should be brought to extinction in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder; yet, although all these sentient beings have been thus extinguished, not a single sentient being has been extinguished.'"
For what reason? If, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva were to give rise to the notion of a sentient being, he should not be called a "bodhisattva mahāsattva."
Even until the perception of a person arises, one should not speak of them as a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Why is that? Because, Subhūti, they do not exist.
There is one dharma, Subhūti, which is the designation for the setting forth of the bodhisattva vehicle.
What do you think about this? Subhūti!
“There is one dharma by which, if the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara were in the presence of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, he would realize unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
When this had been said, [the Buddha continued:]
Then the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One in this way:
“There is no such thing, Blessed One;
there is not even a single dharma that the Tathāgata Dipaṃkara realized as unexcelled perfect enlightenment in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.”
When this had been said,
the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti as follows: "So it is, so it is!
"Subhūti! It is so, it is so!
There is not even a single dharma by which a Tathāgata, acting as a lamp, might realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment in the presence of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Furthermore, Subhūti,
if there were even a single dharma that the Tathāgata had realized and awakened to, I would not have declared of myself as a Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha: "O practitioner, in a future age you shall be a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni."

Therefore, Subhūti, there is not a single dharma that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has realized as unexcelled perfect enlightenment; for that reason, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara predicted of me: "You shall become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha."
“O practitioner, in a future age, you shall be named Śākyamuni, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
For what reason is this?
The Tathāgata, Subhūti, is suchness;
this is precisely who the Tathāgata is, Subhūti.
Subhūti, because it is the dharma of non-arising,
this is itself the World-Honored One; Subhūti,
because it is the severance of the path, this is itself the World-Honored One.
"O Subhūti, because the Tathāgata is ultimately unarisen,
he is such. For what reason?"
Thus, in the ultimate sense, that is truly unarisen.
"If, Subhūti, someone were to speak these words:..."
‘The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment’—that is not according to fact; he slanders me.
That person, Subhūti!
It is an unreal grasping.
For what reason?
Because that does not exist, Subhūti!
There is one dharma, Subhūti, which the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has realized as unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

If, Subhūti, that dharma realized and taught by the Tathāgata were real and not false, for that reason the Tathāgata would say: [it is a dharma]. But because it is neither real nor false, therefore the Tathāgata says: [it is a dharma].
"All dharmas are Buddha-dharmas.
For what reason is that so?
Subhūti, all dharmas, all dharmas—[are indeed Buddha-dharmas].
"All those are non-dharmas," the Tathāgata has said;
therefore, they are called "all dharmas.
"For example, Subhūti!"
"A man possesses a complete body, a great body.
The Venerable Subhūti said:
"If that is so, World-Honored One!"
"Tathāgata, Great Being, you speak of the 'endowed body' and the 'great body';
yet, World-Honored One, you say that it is 'no-body'."
"For that reason, he is called the One with Complete Body and the Great Body.
The World-Honored One said: "So it is, so it is!"
"Subhūti! It is so, it is so!
If a bodhisattva speaks thus:"
"There are sentient beings who enter parinirvāṇa and attain liberation"—
I do not say that such a person is called a bodhisattva.
For what reason?
“Is there, Subhūti,
even one dharma that can be called ‘a bodhisattva’?
Subhūti replied:
"Not so, Blessed One! The Blessed One said:
"Sentient beings, sentient beings, Subhūti!"
"They are not beings; they were spoken of as such by the Tathāgata.
For that reason, they are called 'beings.
For that reason, the Tathāgata said:"
"All dharmas are without self; they are without a sentient being, without a life-span, without a nourisher, and without a person among all dharmas. If, Subhūti!
When a bodhisattva says,
"My buddha-field is accomplished with such adornments," he likewise does not speak in accordance with reality.
For what reason?
Subhūti, that which is called the "adornment of the buddha-field" is, as taught by the Tathāgata, not an adornment.
It is thus called the "adornment of the buddha-field."
For that reason, they are called "adornments of the buddha-field. If, Subhūti,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva has faith and understanding in the selflessness of phenomena and the selflessness of dharmas, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha designates them as a "bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Does the Tathāgata possess a fleshly eye?"
Subhūti said: “So it is, so it is,
World-Honored One!”
"There is the Tathāgata’s fleshly eye.
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think?"
"Subhūti!
Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye?
Subhūti replied:
"So it is, so it is! World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the divine eye."
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
“Is there such a thing as the Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom? Subhūti replied, “It is so, it is so!”
“World-Honored One!
There is the Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom.
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?"
Subhūti said: “So it is, so it is,
World-Honored One!”
"He possesses the Tathāgata’s Dharma-eye.
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think?"
“Subhūti,
does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
Subhūti replied:
"So it is, so it is! World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye."
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!"
What do you think, Subhūti?
Are all those grains of sand in the great river Gaṅgā what the Tathāgata has called "grains of sand"?
Subhūti said: “So it is, so it is!
World-Honored One!”
"So it is, so it is! Well-gone One, you have spoken of that Tathāgata as 'sand.
The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
As many grains of sand as there are in all those great rivers, the Ganges— the number of worlds that would exist corresponding to those grains of sand, would they be many?"
Subhūti said:
“Much, World-Honored One! Much, Sugata!”
"That world exists," the Blessed One said. "It exists, Subhūti!"
In that world-system, I know the various streams of mind of those sentient beings.
For what reason?
Subhūti, as for these "streams of mind," they are streams of mind. Subhūti!
This is not a continuous flow, as taught by the Tathāgata;
for that reason, it is called the "flow of mind.
What is the cause for this?
"In the past, Subhūti, the mind cannot be apprehended;
in the future, the mind cannot be apprehended; in the present, the mind cannot be apprehended.
What do you think?"

"Subhūti! If some son of good family or daughter of good family were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven precious gems and give it as a gift, would that son of good family or daughter of good family generate a great mass of merit on that account?"
Subhūti said:
“Much, World-Honored One! Much, Sugata!”
The Blessed One said:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! So it is, so it is!"
Much, Subhūti!
If that son of good family or daughter of good family were to have that as their object, a great mass of merit would arise—immeasurable and incalculable.
As for "a mass of merit, a mass of merit," Subhūti: [it is so called because it is beyond measure].
That which the Tathāgata has called a "heap" is, in fact, not a heap;
it is for that reason that it is called a "heap of merit.
Furthermore, Subhūti!
"There is a mass of merit," as the Tathāgata has said,
"a mass of merit. What do you think, Subhūti?
“Can a Tathāgata be seen by means of the accomplishment of the form-body?
Subhūti replied, “Not so, World-Honored One!”
One should not perceive a Tathāgata by means of the accomplishment of the form-body.
For what reason?
Because, World-Honored One, the accomplishment of the form-body is merely the accomplishment of the form-body.
"It is 'non-attainment,' as taught by the Tathāgata;
for that reason, it is called 'the attainment of the form-body.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Should one view the Tathāgata as being endowed with the marks of physical perfection?"
Subhūti said: "Not so, World-Honored One!
It is not by means of the possession of marks that a Tathāgata should be perceived."
For what reason is this?
World-Honored One,
that which the Tathāgata has described as "endowment with marks" [is so].
"The Tathāgata has said that 'perfection of physical marks' is not perfection of physical marks;
for that reason, it is called 'perfection of physical marks.
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Nevertheless, the Tathāgata thinks thus:"
"I teach the Dharma," [he said].
Subhūti replied:
"Not so, Blessed One!
It is not as if one should think thus:
'I am teaching the Dharma.'"
The World-Honored One said: "If I, Subhūti,
were to speak thus:"
"He slanders me by saying, 'The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma,' Subhūti!"
It is an unreal grasping.
For what reason?
Subhūti, it is because one speaks of dharmas as dharmas. Subhūti!
“There is no dharma, nor is there any dharma that can be designated as ‘attainable.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One in this way:
“Nevertheless, Blessed One!”

In the future, will there perhaps be sentient beings who, at a later time, a later long period, during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is being destroyed and the times have changed, having heard such a teaching of the Dharma as this, will believe that it truly exists?
The Blessed One said:
"Not so, Subhūti! These beings are not non-beings."
For what reason?
Subhūti, those who are called "sentient beings," all of them are not sentient beings;
they were so described by the Tathāgata.
For that reason, they are called "sentient beings.
What do you think, Subhūti?
"Nevertheless, is there any dharma that has been realized by the Tathāgata as unexcelled, perfect,
and complete enlightenment? Subhūti replied,
"There is none, Blessed One."
"There is a dharma such as the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Blessed One said, "So it is, so it is!"
“Subhūti! It is so, it is so!
Within that, not even the slightest dharma exists or can be found; for that reason, it is called ‘unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.’”
Furthermore, Subhūti, although the true Dharma is equal, there is no inequality within it; for that reason, it is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Because there is no self, no life-principle, no sentient being, and no person, it is equal.
One realizes and awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through all wholesome dharmas.
"Subhūti, as for 'wholesome dharmas,' those which the Tathāgata has called 'wholesome dharmas' are, in fact, not dharmas;
it is for that reason they are called 'wholesome dharmas.'"
"Furthermore, Subhūti!

Suppose one were to take all the Sumeru kings of mountains within the trichiliocosm, and having gathered them all together as a mass of the seven precious jewels, were to scatter them everywhere as a gift to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."

If one has reached the other shore of this wisdom and, having received even a single four-line verse, explains it in detail for others—Subhūti, this accumulation of merit surpasses that previous accumulation of merit;

it does not come within a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-million-hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-billion-hundred-thousandth part, nor a hundred-quintillionth part, nor a fraction, nor a count, nor a calculation, nor a comparison, nor a likeness, nor even a metaphorical illustration.
"What do you think, Subhūti?
Nevertheless, the Tathāgata thinks thus:"
"Do you think, Subhūti, that [the Tathāgata thinks], 'I have delivered sentient beings'?
Furthermore, Subhūti!
One should view it in this way.
For what reason?
Because of existence and non-existence, Subhūti!
There is not a single sentient being whom the Tathāgata has delivered.
Furthermore, Subhūti,
if there were any such sentient beings whom the Tathāgata had delivered, [then that would be so].
In that way, Subhūti, there is for the Tathāgata the grasping of a self, the grasping of a sentient being, the grasping of a life-span, and the grasping of a person.
There is the grasping of a self, O Subhūti, and one who grasps at a self.
"This is not grasping," the Tathāgata has said;
yet those childish, ordinary worldlings give rise to grasping.
"Childish, ordinary worldlings," Subhūti, is what they are called.
"That which is 'not born,' the Tathāgata has preached;
for that reason, it is called a 'childish, ordinary person who is born. What do you think?"
"Subhūti,
could a Tathāgata be seen by means of the possession of marks?
Subhūti replied:
"It is not so, Blessed One!
According to my understanding of the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, I should not see the Tathāgata by means of the possession of marks.
The Blessed One said:
“Excellent, excellent,
Subhūti! It is so, it is so!”
Subhūti! As I have told you, one should not perceive a Tathāgata by means of the perfection of marks.
For what reason?
Furthermore, Subhūti,
one should not see the Tathāgata by means of the possession of physical marks;
for there is no such thing as a wheel-turning monarch, nor is there a Tathāgata.
"Therefore, the Tathāgata should be seen as not possessing these marks.
Because these marks are non-marks, the Tathāgata should be seen.
Then, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One in this way:
“Just as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, Blessed One, I do not see one who is endowed with the marks as being a Tathāgata.
At that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"If one views me through form, or seeks me through sound, practicing a perverted path toward liberation, one does not see me.
One should view the Buddha as the essence of the Dharma; that Tathāgata is the Dharma-body."
Because the nature of phenomena and non-cognition [are such], he is unable to know them.
"What do you think, Subhūti?"
"Is the Tathāgata’s realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment [to be seen] as being endowed with marks?
No, moreover, Subhūti!
It should be viewed in this way."
For what reason? It is not so, Subhūti;
it is not by means of the perfection of physical marks that a Tathāgata awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, Subhūti, at that time there will be those who speak thus:
"For one who has set out on the bodhisattva vehicle, there is a dharma that is destroyed, a designation that is cut off."
"No, Subhūti, it should not be viewed in that way.
For what reason?"
There is no dharma that perishes for one who has set out in the Bodhisattva vehicle; rather, it is established as being uninterrupted.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to fill worlds as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā with the seven treasures and give them as a gift; [if they were to do so...]"
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains patience regarding phenomena within the context of non-self and non-arising,
such a condition will give rise to a vast accumulation of merit.
"No, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should not grasp at a heap of merit. Subhūti said:
"No, World-Honored One!
Should the bodhisattva's mass of merit be grasped?
The World-Honored One said:
“Subhūti, it should be grasped;
Subhūti, it should not be grasped. For that reason, it is called ‘should be grasped.
Nevertheless, furthermore, Subhūti...”
If there should be such speech as:
"The Tathāgata goes, or does not go, or stands, or sits, or lies down, or acts according to the Dharma," Subhūti, that is not mine.
This is called the explanation of the meaning. For what reason?
Subhūti, as for the Tathāgata...
It is called "neither going nor coming"; for that reason, it is called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, Subhūti!

Noble son, or noble daughter, suppose all the dust particles of the earth in a trichiliocosm were ground into ink of such a kind, until it became as numerous as those [particles], like the smallest possible heap.
What do you think, Subhūti?
Does that collection of atoms constitute a great mass?
Subhūti said: “So it is, so it is,
World-Honored One!”
That which constitutes the smallest aggregate of those [atoms] exists.
What is the reason for that?
That, Blessed One!
"World-Honored One, you have not taught that there is a smallest aggregate.
For what reason is this so?
If it is so, World-Honored One..."
It is called the "smallest aggregate" because it is taught as such; yet it is not an aggregate, for the Tathāgata has said so,
and therefore it is designated by the name "smallest aggregate."
When the Tathāgata speaks of a "trichiliocosm," it is not a world-system that the Tathāgata speaks of;
for that reason, he calls it a "trichiliocosm."
What is the reason for that?
World-Honored One,
because the elements exist, there is such grasping at a mass.
If it were so, the Tathāgata would have taught "grasping";
rather, that which the Tathāgata taught was "non-grasping," and for that reason it is called "the grasper."
The Blessed One said:
"Grasping it thus, Subhūti, is not according to worldly convention;
it cannot be described, it is neither dharma nor non-dharma, yet foolish ordinary people give rise to such grasping."
For what reason?
If this exists, Subhūti,
it is said thus:
“I teach the view of a self; Subhūti, I teach the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, and the view of a person.
Nevertheless, Subhūti!
“Is this the correct way of speaking?
Subhūti replied, “Not so, World-Honored One.”
"Not so, Sugata! What is the reason for this?
If that were so, Blessed One..."
What the Tathāgata calls the view of a self is,
in fact, not a view; it is for this reason that the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "view of a self."
The Blessed One said:
"It is so, Subhūti! Those who have set out on the bodhisattva vehicle should know all dharmas, should see them, and should resolve upon them with faith."
Just as with faith and understanding, one likewise abides in the absence of the notion of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*).
For what reason?
Subhūti, that which is called the "notion of phenomena" is [itself] a notion of phenomena.
"Non-perception," this is what the Tathāgata has taught;
for that reason, it is called the "perception of phenomena.
Furthermore, at that time, Subhūti!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, having reached the perfection of wisdom in this manner, were to fill immeasurable and incalculable worlds with the seven treasures and offer them to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; and if another were to receive, analyze, recite, and for others extensively explain and analyze even as much as a single four-line verse [of this teaching]—[the latter would generate far greater merit].
In this way, through that condition, a great mass of merit arises—immeasurable and incalculable. How so?
And what is its detailed exposition?
Since it is not fully expounded here, it is therefore called the "detailed exposition."
“Like a star, a visual fault, a lamp, an illusion, Dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud—
See all conditioned things in this way.”

"World-Honored One, upon hearing these words spoken by the World-Honored One, the Elder Subhūti was filled with joy; and those monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen, as well as the devas, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, were all greatly delighted."
Homage to the ocean of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
The Diamond Cutter Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
